title: Shackleton's Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition
intro: Ernest Shackleton planned the first land crossing of the Antarctic continent, from the Weddell Sea to the Ross Sea. His ship Endurance became trapped in the ice of the Weddell Sea before the party could land, and the expedition became one of survival.
ending: Shackleton, after three failed attempts, brought all the men off Elephant Island on 30 August 1916 without loss of life. The wreck of Endurance was found on the seafloor in 2022.

legs.title: To the ice and the loss of the ship

stops.text: Endurance left Plymouth without Shackleton, who was detained in England by expedition business, and headed first for Buenos Aires.
stops.quote: Endurance, without Shackleton (who was detained in England by expedition business), left Plymouth on 8 August 1914, heading first for Buenos Aires.

stops.text: Shackleton, who had travelled on a faster ship, rejoined the expedition here. The photographer Hurley, Bakewell and the stowaway Blackborow came aboard, and several others left or were discharged. The ship sailed for the South Atlantic on 26 October.
stops.quote: Here Shackleton, who had travelled on a faster ship, rejoined the expedition. Hurley also came on board, together with Bakewell and the stowaway, Blackborow, while several others left the ship or were discharged. On 26 October, the ship sailed for the South Atlantic

stops.text: Endurance reached South Georgia on 5 November and halted for a month at the Grytviken whaling station. She sailed south on 5 December and met pack ice two days later, as far north as 57° 26′S.
stops.quote: After a month-long halt in the Grytviken whaling station on South Georgia, Endurance departed for the Antarctic on 5 December.

legs.title: From the floes to Elephant Island

stops.text: Endurance was held fast in the Weddell Sea ice, drifted north through the winter of 1915 and was abandoned on 27 October 1915. After months on the floes the three lifeboats reached the island, and the James Caird found a narrow shingle beach on its northern shore.
stops.quote: Next day the James Caird rounded the eastern point of the island to reach the northern lee shore, and discovered a narrow shingle beach.

stops.text: The beach would be covered at high tide, so Wild and a crew explored the coast in the Stancomb Wills and found a long spit of land seven miles to the west. The men moved the boats there and later named it Cape Wild.
stops.quote: They returned with news of a long spit of land, seven miles (11 km) to the west. With minimum delay the men returned to the boats and transferred to this new location, which they later christened Cape Wild.

legs.title: The James Caird and the crossing of South Georgia

stops.text: The James Caird was launched from Elephant Island on 24 April 1916 with Shackleton, Worsley, Crean, McNish, Vincent and McCarthy. South Georgia was sighted on 8 May, and two days later the party struggled ashore here.
stops.quote: Two days later, after a prolonged struggle with heavy seas and hurricane-force winds to the south of the island, the party struggled ashore at King Haakon Bay.

stops.text: Shackleton, Worsley and Crean crossed the unexplored interior of the island on a march of 36 hours and reached the whaling station. The whalers met them with shock and disbelief, and the factory manager Thoralf Sørlle gave them food, clothes and shelter.
stops.quote: At seven o'clock in the morning, they heard a steam whistle sound from Stromness, "the first sound created by an outside human agency that had come to our ears since we left Stromness Bay in December 1914".

stops.text: Shackleton left South Georgia on the whaler Southern Sky, but pack ice blocked the way about 70 miles from Elephant Island and the ship retreated here. He cabled London for a ship and was told that none was available before October.
stops.quote: The Southern Sky was not built for ice breaking, and retreated to Port Stanley in the Falkland Islands.

stops.text: After the trawler Instituto de Pesca No. 1 failed to get through the pack, Shackleton, Worsley and Crean came here and met Allan MacDonald, who equipped the schooner Emma. She sailed on 12 July and was also defeated by the ice.
stops.quote: In search of another ship, Shackleton, Worsley and Crean travelled to Punta Arenas, where they met Allan MacDonald, the British owner of the schooner Emma. McDonald equipped this vessel for a further rescue attempt, which left on 12 July

stops.text: The Chilean tug Yelcho, captained by Luis Pardo, left on 25 August and found open seas. The fog lifted at 11:40 a.m. on 30 August and the camp was spotted. Within an hour all the men were aboard.
stops.quote: At 11:40 a.m. on 30 August, the fog lifted, the camp was spotted and, within an hour, all the Elephant Island party were safely aboard, bound for Punta Arenas.

stops.text: Yelcho returned here with all the men from Elephant Island and received a triumphal welcome after its successful mission.
stops.quote: Yelcho had a "triumphal" welcome in Punta Arenas after its successful mission.

stops.text: The rescued men were moved to the port of Valparaíso, where they again had a warm welcome, and from there they were repatriated.
stops.quote: The rescuees were then moved to the port of Valparaíso in Central Chile, where they had again a warm welcome; from there they were repatriated.

notes: Single journey of the Weddell Sea party; the Ross Sea party is left out (the article gives Hobart, McMurdo Sound, Cape Evans, Hut Point with dates, but it is a separate party and was not asked for as a leg beyond need). Positions on the drifting ice (the beset ship, Ocean Camp, Patience Camp) are not stops; they are in the Elephant Island text. Left out: Vahsel Bay, Paulet Island, Deception Island (never reached), Husvik, Montevideo (named only for the loan of Instituto de Pesca). Plymouth: places.tsv has only Plymouth Sound and Plymouth, Montserrat, so entry null; Punta Arenas null (places.tsv Puntarenas is in Costa Rica). Years 1914 for 5 December and 1916 for April dates are inferred from context; Elephant Island date 15 April is 'next day' after 14 April; Cape Wild 16 April likewise. 'Wp' for Stromness is Stromness, South Georgia. The article says the 14 April boats lay off the south-east coast. The arrival at Elephant Island text summarises the drift from nearby lines (abandon 27 October 1915). Elephant Island is visited twice (arrival and rescue).
